1) the success of gene therapy experiments is highly variable and unpredictable, and 2) the variability in the contribution of marked cells over time can be minimized by transplanting large numbers of hematopoietic progenitor cells.
the in vivo biology of HSC must always be considered when designing protocols for gene therapy in large animal models.
the success or failure of a gene therapy experiment is not necessarily related to the technical aspects of the protocol, but is more related to the in vivo biology of the transplanted cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of computer simulation to model the behavior of hematopoietic cells in the context of gene therapy.
the development of gene therapy for genetic disease, with a focus on the use of autologous hematopoietic progenitor cells as a vehicle for gene delivery.
the biology of hematopoietic progenitors and the application of this knowledge to clinical hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT).

the in vivo biology of HSC must always be taken into consideration when designing gene therapy protocols.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the number of transplanted cells and the time after transplantation are critical parameters in determining whether a successful outcome can be achieved in a given animal.
the biology of the HSC is a critical factor in determining the success or failure of a gene therapy experiment.
the number and frequency of transplanted HSPCs, and their in vivo expansion and differentiation behavior are critical to successful gene therapy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is important to understand the biology of the cell type being targeted by gene therapy and to consider the impact of the biology on the experimental design.
it is important to consider the biology of the cells you are trying to modify when you design a clinical trial.
the in vivo biology of hematopoietic cells, particularly hematopoietic progenitors, needs to be considered in the design of any gene therapy experiment.
